Experiment report · VGGT-Omega · Aria fisheye

Filling the black corners does not buy what we hoped

Straightening a fisheye photo leaves black wedges in the corners. We filled them with the real scene — the best any method could do. It bought a little depth accuracy, nothing on camera pose, and less than simply cropping the black away.

96 frames · 12 windows · 4 sequences VGGT-Omega-1B-512, no fine-tuning one run, 2026-09-08
Summary

Four questions

Q1
Does real content in the corners improve depth? Yes, a little. But it helps the fisheye frame as much as the straightened one — so this is not about looking like a normal photo. -0.0152 fisheye · -0.0174 rectified · difference between them -0.0022, could be zero
Q2
Does it improve the camera estimate? No. On fisheye it makes it worse. Pose score -0.040 fisheye · -0.010 rectified · inferred field of view moves 0.6° and stays 17° wrong
Q3
How much of the gain needs a clever filler? Almost none. Smearing the nearest pixel outward gets most of it. Smearing captures 77–126% · at most 0.004 AbsRel left for anything smarter
Q4
Is a wide filled view better than cropping the black away? No. Cropping wins on depth, on pose, and on multi-frame. The gap grows with more frames. Depth 0.0088 better at 1 frame, 0.0228 at 8 · pose 0.98 vs 0.74 · trajectory 0.9 cm vs 7.3 cm

Brackets are 95% confidence intervals. Real means the interval excludes zero. Intervals resample windows, not frames — why.

Part 1 — Motivation

Why fill the corners at all

A fisheye lens draws a circle on a square sensor. The corners hold nothing.

Straightening that circle into a flat photo makes it worse. To keep the whole circle you zoom out, and a third of the frame becomes black wedges.

3D models are trained on ordinary photos. Ordinary photos have no black wedges.

The claim we tested

Fill the wedges → the picture looks normal again → the model works out its own camera → depth improves.

That predicts something specific: filling should help the straightened frame much more than the raw fisheye frame, because only the straightened one becomes a normal photo. If both improve equally, the effect is just "no large black regions" — a much smaller story.

Worth measuring before building. A good filler means a generative model: expensive to build, expensive to run, hard to trust.

Part 2 — Data

Why the frames had to be rendered

You need to know the right answer in the corners. Real footage cannot give it — the lens never pointed there. On real frames you can only compare one guess with another.

So we rebuilt the scene. Four Aria Digital Twin sequences, re-rendered in Blender from their 3D reconstructions (354 objects, 43 lights fitted to the real photos), along the real camera path. Each frame is rendered as a 360° panorama, then resampled into every input below. Depth comes from the renderer, so it is exact and shared.

This gives true content in directions the lens never imaged. That is the ceiling. No filler can beat it.

The inputs

Same instant, same camera, same panorama. They differ only in how it was sampled and what sits in the corners.

1 Raw · black

the fisheye frame as the camera gives it, black in the corners
black 16.0% · scored 85%

2 Rectified · black

straightened to a flat photo, black wedges where nothing was imaged
black 33.5% · scored 68%

3 Raw · filled

same fisheye frame, corners filled with the real scene
black 1.7% · scored 85%

4 Rectified · filled

straightened, wedges filled with the real scene
black 2.1% · scored 68%

5 Cropped

straightened at a narrower zoom, so no black exists at all
black 1.4% · scored 100%

5b Cropped · blurred

input 5 softened to input 4's level of detail
a control, not one of the four cells

  • Inputs 1 and 3 share a field of view. So do 2 and 4. That is the 2×2: projection × corners.
  • The leftover black in 3, 4 and 5 (under 2.1%) is shadow in a dim apartment, not missing render. Every input has it.
  • 96 frames = 4 sequences × 3 windows × 8 frames. Each window covers 2–2.5 m of walking, so eight frames carry real parallax.
Part 3 — Method

How it was scored

VGGT-Omega-1B-512, released weights, no fine-tuning. Run twice over the same frames: one frame at a time, and eight at a time.

Three traps, and how each was closed

TrapFix
Scoring the filled input on more pixels than the black one — it would win just by covering more. Both halves of a pair are scored on the black one's region. Filled pixels are never compared against anything.
Comparing inputs that see different amounts of the world. Input 5 sees a narrower slice than input 4. Every comparison with input 5 is also run with all inputs restricted to input 5's slice, computed from each pixel's ray. Both versions are reported.
Treating 96 frames as 96 samples. The 8 frames of a window share a room, a light setup and half a second of walking. Every interval resamples whole windows (n = 12). Wider, and honest.

What is measured

  • Depth. AbsRel — average relative error after removing the model's unknown scale and offset. Lower is better. Plus δ₁, the fraction of pixels within 25% of truth. Higher is better.
  • Camera pose. Per 8-frame window, every pair of frames compared through its relative pose, so the model's free origin and scale cannot help it. AUC@30 summarises how many pairs get rotation and translation direction right (0–1, higher better). ATE is trajectory error in centimetres.
  • Field of view. What the model thinks its lens is. Truth is 124.7° for inputs 2 and 4, 106.8° for input 5. Fisheye inputs have no pinhole truth, so their number is shown but not graded.

The ground-truth camera convention was checked on the data, not read off a comment: reprojecting one frame's depth into the next lands within 0.12% median error, against 4–7% for each alternative.

Result 1 — filling helps depth a little, and both projections equally

Black cornersFilled with truthAbsRel change [95% interval]Verdict

Rectified, 8 frames0.06980.0595-0.0102 [-0.0173, -0.0026]filling is better

AbsRel: average relative depth error. Lower is better. Compare rows within a projection, not across it — the fisheye and rectified grids sample the world differently.

Filling helps, in all four rows. Now the actual test: does it help the rectified frame more than the fisheye one?

Is the rectified gain bigger than the fisheye gain?Fisheye gainRectified gainGap between them [95% interval]Verdict
1 frame-0.0152-0.0174-0.0022 [-0.0144, +0.0129]no
8 frames-0.0176-0.0102+0.0074 [-0.0114, +0.0333]no

The prediction fails. The two gains are the same size, the gap includes zero in both modes, and it even flips sign between them. Across three metrics and two modes: six gains are real, six gaps are not.

The gain sits in a narrow band just inside the edge of the black. Within 16 pixels of that edge, error drops 42% (fisheye) and 47% (rectified). Further in, only 15% and 15%. A boundary effect, the same size in both projections.

All from 8-frame windows. Rectified: nothing changes. Fisheye: filling makes the camera worse on all three.

A reading, not a measurement: the filled fisheye corners are real scene content placed beyond the angle the lens can physically image — a lens no real camera has. The depth head sees extra texture and gains; the camera head sees an impossible lens and loses.

The field of view explains it

Each input has its own true field of view. Inputs 2 and 4 share one, because filling the wedges does not change how wide the frame is. Input 5 is a different, narrower camera — so it must be compared against its own number, not theirs. The fisheye inputs are not pinhole images at all: there is no pinhole field of view for them to be right about, so their reading is listed but not graded.

InputTrue field of viewModel says (1 frame)Off by
1 Raw · blacknone — spans 112° across its axes86.5°—
2 Rectified · black124.7°106.9°17.8°
3 Raw · fillednone — spans 112° across its axes83.8°—
4 Rectified · filled124.7°107.5°17.2°
5 Cropped106.8°101.4°5.4°

The finding that settles the original idea

A clean, black-free 125° photo is still read as 108° — off by 17°. Filling moves that guess by 0.6°.

The model is not confused by the black. It does not recognise the width. Filling changes the corners; it does not change the width.

The frames are square with equal focal lengths, so horizontal and vertical field of view are the same number. The model emits both; they agree within 0.8°. The vertical one is plotted.

Result 3 — cheap filling already takes nearly all of it

How much of the gain does the dumbest filler get for free? "Smeared" repeats the nearest real pixel outward. It invents nothing. All four numbers in a row are AbsRel on the same pixels — the only thing that changes is what went into the corners.

BlackSmearedReal sceneLeft for a smarter filler
Fisheye, 1 frame0.08610.07350.0709+0.0026
Rectified, 1 frame0.07680.06330.0594+0.0039
Fisheye, 8 frames0.09870.08180.0811+0.0007
Rectified, 8 frames0.06980.05690.0595-0.0026

Read one row left to right. Black is worst. Smearing recovers most of the distance. The real scene adds only the last column, which is the entire budget for a generative filler: at most 0.004 AbsRel. In the bottom row that budget is negative — smearing already beats the truth, because real corner detail is complicated, a smear is simple, and the model prefers simple.

Incidental, but worth carrying: a flat grey fill helps on a rectified frame (0.0768 → 0.0650) and is much worse than black on a raw fisheye (0.0861 → 0.1204). Fill advice does not transfer across projections.

Result 4 — cropping beats a wide filled view

Input 5 sidesteps the problem: zoom in until the black is outside the frame. It costs ~17% of the lens's solid angle, and needs no filler, no model, no compute. That is what filling has to beat.

But inputs 4 and 5 differ in two things: the field of view, and how many pixels each spends on the part they share (input 5 all of them, input 4 about half — a factor of 1.42). So input 5 might just be sharper. Input 5b settles it: input 5 band-limited to input 4's sampling rate. Same framing, input 4's detail.

No. Blurring input 5 to input 4's level of detail changes almost nothing. One row is real but tiny — 0.0011, about 20× smaller than the gap with input 4 — and it points the wrong way: the blurred version is very slightly better.

Cropping wins by 0.0088 AbsRel at 1 frame and 0.0228 at 8 — a 2.6× wider gap. The control 5b lands on 5 everywhere (pose 0.981 against 0.980). Sharpness explains none of it.

Input 4 carries strictly more of the scene than input 5. If extra context were what multi-frame needs, input 4 should gain most. It gains least. Compared window by window, input 5 gains +0.0140 [+0.0055, +0.0225] real more than input 4. On the filled fisheye, eight frames are actively worse than one.

A tempting explanation that failed its test

"Multi-frame only pays where the camera is right" fits the headline numbers. Tested properly, it does not hold.

Across 192 (input × window) combinations, the correlation between a window's multi-frame gain and its camera score is -0.12 overall, and +0.13 once each window is centred — the level at which the mechanism would have to work. The multi-frame results above are description, not a demonstrated cause.

What it looks like

Part 5 — Conclusion

What to do

Recommendation

Do not build a generative filler for this. The whole prize is 0.015–0.017 AbsRel. A smear that invents nothing already takes 77%+ of it. None of it reaches the camera estimate, which was the point.

Crop instead of filling. It costs ~17% of the lens's solid angle and beats the filled wide version on depth, on camera pose, and on multi-frame gain.

The reason underneath: the model does not fail because the picture has black in it. It fails because the picture is wide. A clean 125° photo is read as 108°; a 107° one is read almost right. Filling changes the corners, not the width.

What this does not settle

  • Where the limit is. We tested two zoom levels: 107° works, 125° does not. The transition could be anywhere between. Cheap to find — same renders, one parameter.
  • Training-based approaches. Calibration tokens (Fisheye3R) and positional-encoding adapters (RayTun3R) attack the width, not the black. This experiment does not argue against them. It does sharpen their target: keep the whole lens and match what cropping gets free (0.98 vs 0.74; 0.9 cm vs 7.3 cm).
  • Rendered ≠ real. Lighting was fitted to the real frames. An earlier badly-lit render of the same geometry gave the same conclusions with effects 4–6× larger — directions are robust, magnitudes are a property of the render.
  • One model, one scene type. VGGT-Omega-1B-512, furnished apartment. Nothing checked on another backbone or outdoors.
